content: In 1976, the American Thoracic Society (ATS) released concise guidelines for the investigation, diagnostic evaluation, and medical treatment of tuberculosis (TB) contacts. Despite TB elimination being a national priority, second only to treating individuals with active TB disease, these guidelines have not been updated since their initial publication. The current statement, jointly issued by the National Tuberculosis Controllers Association (NTCA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), was developed by a working group composed of members from both organizations. This group based their recommendations on a thorough review of relevant epidemiological and scientific studies, as well as established practices in conducting contact investigations. The statement provides expanded guidelines for investigating TB exposure and transmission, as well as preventing future TB cases through contact investigations. It also addresses data management, confidentiality, consent, and human resource considerations. These guidelines are primarily intended for public health officials but are also relevant to others involved in TB control efforts. While the recommendations are tailored to the United States, they may be adaptable for use in other countries that follow guidelines issued by the World Health Organization (WHO), the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease, or national TB control programs. Contact investigations are inherently complex, requiring numerous interdependent decisions, often made with incomplete data, and involving time-intensive interventions. Successful decision-making during these investigations necessitates the use of a multifactorial approach rather than simple decision trees. Factors such as the extent of disease in the index patient, the duration and proximity of exposure, and local air circulation have been confirmed to influence transmission risk. However, other factors, such as the infectious burden of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, prior exposure, strain virulence, and individual susceptibility, remain less well understood. No safe duration of exposure to airborne M. tuberculosis has been established. Even brief exposure carries a theoretical risk of infection, as a single bacterium can initiate disease. Public health officials must prioritize resources to identify exposed individuals who are most likely to be infected or develop TB disease. These guidelines provide a framework for gathering information and making informed decisions during contact investigations, while emphasizing the importance of experienced judgment. Practical considerations, such as the availability of resources (primarily personnel), are also taken into account. The working group reviewed scientific literature and established practices to develop these recommendations. Although a controlled trial has demonstrated the efficacy of treating infected contacts with isoniazid (INH), the effectiveness of contact investigations themselves has not been established through controlled trials. Consequently, the recommendations reflect expert opinion derived from common practices that have not been critically tested. These guidelines are not universally applicable and must be adapted to specific circumstances. For example, investigations involving children or immunocompromised individuals may warrant special consideration. The statement is organized into 13 sections, covering topics such as initiating contact investigations, investigating index patients and transmission sites, assigning priorities to contacts, diagnostic and public health evaluations, medical treatment for latent TB infection (LTBI), and expanding investigations when necessary. It also addresses communication with the media, data management, confidentiality, staffing and training, special circumstances, source-case investigations, and other specialized topics. Key points include: Decisions to initiate contact investigations should prioritize index patients with positive acid-fast bacillus (AFB) sputum smears or pulmonary cavities. The use of nucleic acid amplification (NAA) tests is also discussed. Investigating the index patient involves gathering comprehensive information, including medical history, treatment initiation, and drug susceptibility results. Written policies and procedures improve the efficiency and consistency of investigations. Assigning priorities to contacts is based on individual characteristics and exposure features. High-priority contacts include those in households, congregate living settings, or exposed during cough-inducing medical procedures. Diagnostic evaluation includes specific recommendations for children under five years old and immunocompromised individuals, who should undergo chest radiographs. The recommended interval between exposure and final tuberculin skin testing has been revised to 8–10 weeks. Effective contact investigations require completion of therapy, which remains a significant challenge for both patients and healthcare providers. Treatment should focus on highand medium-priority contacts. Expanding investigations may be necessary when new information arises or when initial low-priority contacts are reclassified as higher priority. Communication with the media can enhance public knowledge of TB control efforts and the role of health departments. Data management emphasizes electronic storage and the use of data to assess the effectiveness of investigations. Confidentiality and consent are critical in maintaining trust and protecting patient privacy. Staffing and training are essential for conducting effective investigations. Personnel should be trained in interview techniques and supported with on-the-job mentoring. Special circumstances, such as investigations in schools, hospitals, or workplaces, require tailored approaches. Source-case investigations should only be conducted when more urgent investigations have been successfully completed. Their effectiveness and outcomes should be critically monitored due to their general inefficiency. Newly approved blood tests for diagnosing M. tuberculosis infection may improve the science of contact investigations if they prove superior to the tuberculin skin test (TST). The guidelines emphasize the importance of determining the infectious period to focus investigations on contacts most at risk. Practical estimation is necessary, as the start of the infectious period cannot be precisely determined. The infectious period typically begins three months before TB diagnosis but may extend further in cases of prolonged illness. The period ends when effective treatment has been initiated, as evidenced by microbiological improvement and clinical response. Interviews with index patients are critical for setting the direction of the investigation and providing education about TB. The first interview should occur within one business day for infectious patients and within three business days for others. A minimum of two interviews is recommended, with follow-up interviews conducted 1–2 weeks later. Proxy interviews may be necessary when the patient cannot be interviewed, but these must be conducted with clear guidelines to protect confidentiality. Field investigations, including site visits, complement interviews by providing additional information about transmission settings and identifying contacts. Site visits should occur within three days of the initial interview and include observations of physical conditions, such as room size, ventilation, and airflow patterns. These factors contribute to the likelihood of transmission and should be considered alongside the index patient’s behavior and duration of exposure. In summary, these guidelines provide a comprehensive framework for conducting TB contact investigations, balancing scientific evidence with practical considerations and expert judgment. They aim to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of TB control efforts while maintaining respect for patient confidentiality and privacy.
